blocks.title: Welcome to the extended module «Watch or see?»
blocks.body:
This is the **extended module** of the unit «Cate's Sound Lab». It is made for learners who want a bigger challenge – if you are in the extended track, this module is for you; everybody else can use it as extra practice.

You will:

- learn when to use *watch*, *see* and *look at* – three verbs for your **eyes**, just like *listen* and *hear* were for your ears,
- build **past simple** and **past perfect** forms yourself, without answer options,
- complete a longer story about an unforgettable concert.

Take your time, and go back to Module 2 whenever you need the grammar rules again.

blocks.title: Part 1: watch, see or look at?
blocks.body:
All three verbs are about your eyes – but they do different jobs.

**watch** = follow something that **moves**, for a longer time, with attention.

- We **watched** the band's new music video three times in a row.
- Thousands of fans **watched** the drummer's solo on the big screens.

**see** = something comes to your eyes (you don't plan it) – or you **attend** an event: you see a film at the cinema, a concert, a band live.

- I **saw** your sister in the crowd, but she didn't **see** me.
- Next summer we're going to **see** our favourite band live in Zurich.

**look at** = turn your eyes to something **static** – a photo, a poster, a setlist – usually for a short moment.

- **Look at** this old tour poster – it's from 1998!
- She **looked at** the setlist and smiled.

**In short:** moving + longer → *watch* · it just comes to your eyes, or you are in the audience → *see* · static + you turn your eyes to it → *look at*.

One warning for music fans: you usually **watch** a music video, but you **see** a band live or **see** a concert (= you are there). The picture below shows all three.

blocks.title: Three verbs for your eyes
blocks.alt: Chart with three panels. Panel 1, blue, titled «WATCH»: a person sits on a sofa and follows a music video on a screen with a play symbol and music notes. Below: «follow something that moves – for a longer time», example «watch a music video», and the extra line «also: watch TV, watch a film at home». Panel 2, orange, titled «SEE»: a small concert scene with a stage, a singer and an audience. Below: «it comes to your eyes – or you are there», example «see a band live», and the extra line «also: see a concert, see a film at the cinema». Panel 3, green, titled «LOOK AT»: a person turns their eyes to a poster on a wall; a dotted line runs from their eyes to the poster. Below: «turn your eyes to something static», example «look at a poster», and the extra line «also: look at a photo, look at the setlist». A dark bar at the bottom repeats the three collocations – watch a music video · see a band live · look at a poster – and adds the quick test: moving? watch · you are there or it just happens? see · static? look at.
blocks.caption: Three verbs, three jobs: watch follows movement, see happens or means being there, look at aims your eyes at something static.

blocks.title: Exercise 1: watch, see or look at?
blocks.intro: Choose the correct option for each gap. Think about the three jobs: moving, coming to your eyes / being there, or static.

questions.prompt: Quiet, please! We are ___ the new music video right now.
questions.explanation: A music video moves, and you follow it with attention – that is *watch*. *See* is not normally used in the -ing form for this («we are seeing» sounds wrong here), *looking* would need *at* plus a static object, and *watching at* does not exist – *watch* never takes *at*.

questions.prompt: I ___ your sister at the concert yesterday, but there were too many people to say hello.
questions.explanation: She simply came into your view for a moment – you did not plan it and you did not follow her for a long time. That is *see* → *saw*. *Watched* would mean you observed her with attention for a while, *seen* would need *have* or *had* before it, and *watched at* does not exist.

questions.prompt: ___ this old tour poster – my mum was at this show in 1998!
questions.explanation: A poster is static – it does not move. So you turn your eyes to it: *look at*. *Watch at* does not exist (and *watch* is for moving things anyway), *see* is not used as a command like this, and *look* alone is not enough when an object follows.

questions.prompt: Have you ever ___ a concert in a big stadium?
questions.explanation: You *see* a concert – you are there and you experience it (but you *watch* a video at home). After *have you ever …?* you need the past participle, so *seen* is right and *saw* is the wrong form. *Watch* is the wrong form too, and *look at* does not work for a concert.

questions.prompt: Dad ___ the whole three-hour concert film on TV without a single break.
questions.explanation: Three hours of moving pictures, followed with attention from start to finish – that is *watch*. *Look at* is for static things, *saw at* does not exist, and *see* is the wrong form for a finished action in the past.

questions.prompt: The singer stopped and ___ the crowd for a moment before the last song.
questions.explanation: *For a moment* tells you it was short: she turned her eyes to the crowd – *looked at*. *Was watching* would mean following them for a longer time (and does not fit after «stopped and …»), *saw* does not fit a deliberate short glance, and *looked* alone is missing *at*.

blocks.title: Exercise 2: The right verb in the right tense
blocks.intro: Drag the correct form into each gap (on a phone: tap the form first, then the gap): *watch*, *see* or *look at* – in the tense that fits the sentence. **Careful: three forms in the list are wrong forms – they fit nowhere.**
blocks.text:
Every Sunday I {{1}} old concert films on my laptop for hours.
I {{2}} my old schoolmate in the crowd yesterday, but a second later she was gone.
Please {{3}} the stage design in this photo – isn't it amazing?
Before last night, I {{4}} the band live only once, at a tiny festival.
By the time the interview started, half a million people {{5}} the new video.
During the guitar solo, everyone {{6}} the guitarist's hands – nobody wanted to miss a single move.
After the concert, we {{7}} all the photos on Lea's phone, one by one.

blocks.title: Part 2: Quick reminder – past simple and past perfect
blocks.body:
You know this from Module 2: with **two past actions**, the **past perfect** (*had* + past participle) marks the one that happened **first**; the later action takes the **past simple**. Signal words: *before, after, already, by the time, when*.

> When we arrived, the band **had** already **started**.

If you want the full explanation and the big timeline, go back to Module 2 «Listen or hear?». From here on, you build the forms yourself – no answer options any more.

blocks.title: The timeline in one line
blocks.alt: Small timeline strip. An arrow runs from left to right to a dark marker labelled «NOW». A blue dot on the left is labelled «earlier action – past perfect» with the example «the band had started»; an orange dot further right is labelled «later action – past simple» with the example «we arrived». A box under the line shows the rule: past perfect = had + past participle, the same for all persons: I had – she had – we had – they had.
blocks.caption: The short version of the Module 2 timeline – for a quick look while you work.

blocks.title: Exercise 3: Build the form
blocks.intro: Complete each sentence with the verb in brackets. Use the past simple or the past perfect – decide which action came first. Careful: sometimes the gap is the later action!
blocks.text:
By the time we reached the stadium, the show {{1}} (begin).
When we met at six, Mia {{2}} (buy) our tickets already, so we walked straight in.
We {{3}} (go) home by bus after the final song.
I recognised the melody at once, because I {{4}} (hear) it many times before.
By the time the encore {{5}} (begin), some fans had already left the hall.
The band {{6}} (see) the fans' banners and smiled.
Before the doors {{7}} (open), fans had waited in the rain for hours.
It was the best show I {{8}} (see) in my whole life.

blocks.title: Exercise 4: The concert I will never forget
blocks.intro: Read the whole story first. Then complete it: put each verb in brackets into the past simple or the past perfect. The context tells you which event happened earlier.
blocks.text:
Two years ago, my favourite band finally {{1}} (come) to Switzerland.
I {{2}} (want) to see them live for years, so my aunt bought us tickets as a birthday surprise.
When we arrived at the stadium, hundreds of fans {{3}} (take) their places already.
The band {{4}} (play) in our country twice before, but I {{5}} (miss) both shows because I was too young.
At nine o'clock, the lights {{6}} (go) out, and the crowd screamed.
The singer {{7}} (begin) with a quiet song that she {{8}} (write) as a teenager.
By the end of the night, I {{9}} (sing) so loudly that I could hardly speak – but I was the happiest person in the stadium.

blocks.title: Final quiz: eyes, ears and two past tenses
blocks.intro: Six questions from the whole module – vocabulary, grammar, and one look back at Module 2.

questions.prompt: You were at a big show last Saturday and want to tell everyone: «I ___ my favourite band live!»
questions.explanation: Being at a show is *seeing* a band live: «I saw my favourite band live!» Last Saturday is finished, so you need the past form *saw* – *see* is the present form. *Look at* is for static things, and *watched at* does not exist.

options.text: Look at this photo of the stage!
Watch this photo of the stage!
See at this photo of the stage!
Look this photo of the stage!

questions.explanation: A photo is static, so you *look at* it. *Watch* is for moving things, *see* never takes *at*, and *look* without *at* cannot take an object.

questions.prompt: «By midnight, the DJ ___ for six hours.» Which form fills the gap?
questions.explanation: *By midnight* looks back from a point in the past – the playing happened before that point, so you need the past perfect: *had played*. *Has played* is the present perfect, and *plays/play* are present forms.

questions.prompt: «The fans knew every word, because the album had come out months earlier.» – What happened first?

options.text: Both happened at the same time.
The sentence does not tell us.

questions.explanation: *Had come out* is past perfect – the earlier event. First the album came out, months later the fans were at the concert and knew every word.

questions.prompt: A look back at Module 2: «Turn the volume up – I can't ___ the lyrics!»
questions.explanation: This is about what reaches your ears: with *can/can't* you talk about ability – *I can't hear the lyrics*. *Listen (to)* is the active verb and does not fit after *can't* here, and *see* is for your eyes.

options.text: We had saw the band before.
We had see the band before.
We have seen the band before yesterday.
We had seen the band before.

questions.explanation: The past perfect is *had + past participle*, and the participle of *see* is *seen*: «We had seen the band before.» *Had saw* and *had see* use the wrong form, and the present perfect (*have seen*) cannot be combined with a finished past time like *yesterday*.
